![](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/nuke-world-map-2025-scaled.png)

Global Risk

#### *Who owns the world’s nuclear weapons?*

Despite progress in reducing nuclear weapon arsenals since the Cold War, the world’s combined inventory of nuclear warheads remains at a very high level: nine countries possessed roughly 12,187 warheads as of the beginning of 2026.

Combined, the United States and Russia now possess approximately 86 percent of the world’s total inventory of nuclear weapons, and 83 percent of the stockpiled warheads available for use by the military. Currently, no other nuclear-armed state sees a need for more than a few hundred nuclear weapons for national security, although many of these states are increasing their nuclear stockpiles.

Globally, the overall inventory of nuclear weapons is declining, but the pace of reductions is slowing compared with the past 30 years. Moreover, these reductions are happening only because the United States and Russia are still dismantling previously retired warheads.

**In contrast to the overall inventory of nuclear weapons, the number of warheads in global military stockpiles – which comprises warheads assigned to operational forces – is increasing once again.** The United States is still reducing its nuclear stockpile slowly. France and Israel have relatively stable inventories. But China, India, North Korea, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom, as well as possibly Russia, are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles (see map below, [click here](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/nuke-world-map-2025-scaled.png) for higher resolution image):

![](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/nuke-world-map-2025-scaled.png)

Of the world’s approximate 12,187 nuclear warheads, roughly 9,745 are in military stockpiles for use by missiles, aircraft, ships, and submarines. The remaining warheads have been retired but are still relatively intact and are awaiting dismantlement. Of the 9,745 warheads in the military stockpiles, some 3,912 are deployed with operational forces (on missiles or bomber bases). Of those, approximately 2,100 US, Russian, British, and French warheads are on [high alert](http://www.unidir.org/files/publications/pdfs/reducing-alert-rates-of-nuclear-weapons-400.pdf), ready for use on short notice (see table):

Estimated Global Nuclear Warhead Inventories, 2026

Hans M. Kristensen, Matt Korda, Eliana Johns, and Mackenzie Knight-Boyle, Federation of American Scientists, 2026

The exact number of nuclear weapons in each country’s possession is a closely held national secret, so the estimates presented here come with significant uncertainty. Most nuclear-armed states provide essentially no information about the sizes of their nuclear stockpiles. Yet the degree of secrecy varies considerably from country to country. Between 2010 and 2018, the United States disclosed its total stockpile size, but in 2019, the Trump administration [stopped that practice](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2020/12/nuclear-stockpile-denial-2020/). In 2020, the Biden administration [restored nuclear transparency](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2021/10/nuclear-stockpile2021/), but then [declined](https://fas.org/publication/while-advocating-nuclear-transparency-abroad-biden-administration-limits-it-at-home/) to declassify any US stockpile data for 2021, 2022, and 2023, before declassifying the numbers again in [2024](https://fas.org/publication/united-states-discloses-nuclear-warhead-numbers-restores-nuclear-transparency/) – a brief victory for nuclear accountability in a democratic country.

Similarly, in 2021, the United Kingdom [announced](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/global-britain-in-a-competitive-age-the-integrated-review-of-security-defence-development-and-foreign-policy/global-britain-in-a-competitive-age-the-integrated-review-of-security-defence-development-and-foreign-policy) that it would no longer disclose public figures for its operational stockpile, deployed warhead, or deployed missile numbers. In 2023, both the United States and Russia also elected to no longer exchange publicly available data about their deployed strategic warheads and launchers as mandated by the New START Treaty. Most recently, France [announced](https://www.elysee.fr/emmanuel-macron/2026/03/02/deplacement-sur-la-base-operationnelle-de-lile-longue) in early 2026 that it will no longer disclose the figures for its nuclear arsenal as it has in the past.

Despite these limitations, however, publicly available information, careful analysis of historical records, and occasional leaks make it possible to make the best estimates about the size and composition of the national nuclear weapon stockpiles. For a breakdown of the nuclear warhead categories of the different nuclear-armed states, and for links to more detailed overviews of each country’s arsenals, see this table:

Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

| Country | Deployed Strategic | Deployed Nonstrategic | Reserve/Nondeployed | Military Stockpile(a) | Total Inventory(b) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Russia | 1,796(c) | 0(d) | 2,604(e) | 4,400 | 5,420(f) |
| United States | 1,670(g) | 100(h) | 1,930 | 3,700(i) | 5,042(j) |
| France | 280 | n.a. | 10(k) | 290 | 370(l) |
| China | 34 | n.a. | 586 | 620 | 620(m) |
| United Kingdom | 120 | n.a. | 105 | 225 | 225(n) |
| Israel | 0 | n.a. | 90 | 90 | 90(o) |
| Pakistan | 0 | n.a. | 170 | 170 | 170(p) |
| India | 0 | n.a. | 178 | 190 | 190(q) |
| North Korea | 0 | n.a. | 60 | 60 | 60(r) |
| Total(s) | ~3,912 | ~100 | ~5,733 | ~9,745 | ~12,187 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

**How to read this table:** “Deployed strategic warheads” are those deployed on intercontinental missiles and at heavy bomber bases. “Deployed nonstrategic warheads” are those deployed on bases with operational short-range delivery systems. “Reserve/Nondeployed” warheads are those not deployed on launchers but in storage (weapons at bomber bases are considered deployed). The “military stockpile” includes active and inactive warheads that are in the custody of the military and earmarked for use by commissioned deliver vehicles. The “total inventory” includes warheads in the military stockpile as well as retired, but still intact, warheads in the queue for dismantlement. For additional guidance, see endnotes below (**note: as estimates are updated, they may vary from the printed materials below**).

Expand
Footnotes

*a* Warheads in the “military stockpile” are defined as warheads in the custody of the military and earmarked for use by military forces.  
*b* The “total inventory” counts warheads in the military stockpile as well as retired, but still intact, warheads awaiting dismantlement.  
*c* This number is higher than the aggregate data under the now-expired [New START Treaty](https://www.state.gov/new-start-treaty-aggregate-numbers-of-strategic-offensive-arms/) because this table also counts bomber weapons at bomber bases as deployed. [Detailed 2026 overview of Russian forces is here](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/00963402.2026.2659527?needAccess=true). Numbers have been updated for later changes.  
*d* All are declared to be in central storage, although some storage sites may be close to bases with operational forces. Many retired non-strategic warheads are thought to be awaiting dismantlement.  
*e* Includes an estimated 810 strategic warheads and all 1,794 non-strategic warheads.  
*f* In addition to the 4,400 warheads in the military stockpile, an estimated 1,020 retired warheads are thought to be awaiting dismantlement. Public details are scarce, but we estimate that Russia is dismantling 50-200 retired warheads per year. US Strategic Command and part of the Intelligence Community [projected in 2020](https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Richard_02-13-20.pdf) that “Russia’s overall nuclear stockpile is likely to grow significantly over the next decade – growth driven primarily by a projected increase in Russia’s non-strategic nuclear weapons.” So far, however, there is no public evidence of that increase. ([Detailed 2026 overview of Russian nuclear forces is here](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/00963402.2026.2659527?needAccess=true).)  
*g* This number is higher than the aggregate data released under the now-expired [New START treaty](https://www.state.gov/new-start-treaty-aggregate-numbers-of-strategic-offensive-arms/) because this table also counts bomber weapons on bomber bases as deployed. [Detailed 2026 overview of US forces is available here.](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00963402.2026.2633029#abstract)  
*h* Some 100-120 B61 bombs are deployed in Europe at six-seven bases in five-six countries (Belgium, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Turkey, and possibly the United Kingdom).  
*i* The U.S. government [declared](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2018/03/stockpile-reduction/) in March 2018 that its stockpile included 3,822 warheads as of September 2017. After that, the [Trump administration decided](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2020/12/nuclear-stockpile-denial-2020/) no longer to declassify the numbers. In 2021, the Biden administration [declassified](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2021/10/nuclear-stockpile2021/) the number of warheads in the stockpile and the number of dismantled warheads, noting that the stockpile consisted of 3,750 warheads as of September 2020. After two years of rejecting declassification, the Biden administration in 2024 [declassified the number](https://fas.org/publication/united-states-discloses-nuclear-warhead-numbers-restores-nuclear-transparency/): 3,748 warheads as of September 2023. In Since then, additional warheads have been retired for an estimated stockpile of approximately 3,700 warheads.  
*j* In addition to the roughly 3,700 warheads in the military stockpile and the estimated 1,342 retired warheads awaiting dismantlement, roughly 20,000 plutonium cores (pits) and perhaps up to 4,000 Canned Assemblies (secondaries) from dismantled warheads are in storage at the Pantex Plant in Texas and Y-12 plant in Tennessee.   
*k* Weapons for France’s single aircraft carrier are not deployed on the ship under normal circumstances but could be on short notice. Warhead loadings on some submarines missiles have been reduced to increase targeting flexibility. ([Detailed overview of 2025 French nuclear forces is here](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/00963402.2025.2524251?needAccess=true)).  
*l* It is believed that France offloaded the last of its older TN75 warheads from Le Vigilant in late 2023. Given that France’s current priority remains the production of new modified TNO-2 warheads, we assume that up to 80 of these retired TN75 warheads still remain in the queue for eventual dismantlement.

*m* The Chinese stockpile is increasing, and in 2022 the US Department of Defense [claimed](https://media.defense.gov/2022/Nov/29/2003122279/-1/-1/1/2022-MILITARY-AND-SECURITY-DEVELOPMENTS-INVOLVING-THE-PEOPLES-REPUBLIC-OF-CHINA.PDF) that by 2030 China’s nuclear stockpile “will have about 1,000 operational nuclear warheads.” Part of that increase is already well underway and our estimate includes some of it; however, these claims depend on many uncertain factors, including how many missile silos will be built, how many warheads each missile will carry, and assumptions about the future production of fissile materials by China. A small number of the warheads are now thought to be deployed, while the vast majority are kept in storage under central control. China considers all of its nuclear weapons to be strategic, but the US military calls its medium-and intermediate-range missile non-strategic. ([Detailed 2025 overview of Chinese nuclear forces is here](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00963402.2025.2467011). Updated over scheduled for early-July 2026.)

The [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") has [possessed nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_China "Nuclear weapons of China") since 1964. It was the last to develop them of the five [nuclear-weapon states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-weapon_states "Nuclear-weapon states") recognized by the [Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") (NPT). China acceded to the [Biological Weapons Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Weapons_Convention "Biological Weapons Convention") (BWC) in 1984,[[4]](#cite_note-4) acceded to the NPT in 1992,[[5]](#cite_note-5) and ratified the [Chemical Weapons Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_Weapons_Convention "Chemical Weapons Convention") (CWC) in 1997.[[6]](#cite_note-:6-6)

China [tested its first nuclear bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_596 "Project 596") in 1964 and [its first full-scale thermonuclear bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_639 "Project 639") in 1967. It carried out 45 [nuclear tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_weapons_tests_of_China "List of nuclear weapons tests of China") before signing the [Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty") in 1996.

China is estimated to possess a stockpile of approximately 620 nuclear warheads as of 2026,[[1]](#cite_note-FAS_World-1) making it the [third-largest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_with_nuclear_weapons#Estimated_worldwide_nuclear_stockpiles "List of countries with nuclear weapons") in the world. Since 2020, the [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") has operated a [nuclear triad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_triad "Nuclear triad").[[3]](#cite_note-:284-3) Of its 600 warheads, it is estimated 376 are assigned to its [Rocket Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force")'s [*Dongfeng*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongfeng_(missile) "Dongfeng (missile)") [intermediate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate-range_ballistic_missile "Intermediate-range ballistic missile") and [intercontinental ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile "Intercontinental ballistic missile"), 72 to its [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_Navy "People's Liberation Army Navy")'s [*Julang*-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julang_3 "Julang 3") [submarine-launched ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine-launched_ballistic_missile "Submarine-launched ballistic missile") on six [Type 094 submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_094_submarine "Type 094 submarine"), and 20 to its [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_Air_Force "People's Liberation Army Air Force")'s [*Jinglei*-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JL-1_(air-launched_ballistic_missile) "JL-1 (air-launched ballistic missile)") [air-launched ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air-launched_ballistic_missile "Air-launched ballistic missile") for 20 [Xi'an H-6N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi'an_H-6 "Xi'an H-6") [strategic bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bomber "Strategic bomber"). Approximately 132 warheads await assignment. China is upgrading its triad with the in-development [Xi'an H-20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi'an_H-20 "Xi'an H-20") [stealth bomber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stealth_aircraft "Stealth aircraft"), [Type 096 submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_096_submarine "Type 096 submarine"), and large [missile silo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_silo "Missile silo") fields. China fields [multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_independently_targetable_reentry_vehicle "Multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle"), and has tested [hypersonic glide vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_glide_vehicle "Hypersonic glide vehicle") and a [fractional orbital bombardment system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_orbital_bombardment_system "Fractional orbital bombardment system").[[8]](#cite_note-:384-8)

# Lens 1B.1 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler seek to reduce nuclear or other existential risk, rather than increase prestige, leverage, or personal power through escalation?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The evidence for 2023 is mixed but weighted toward escalation / leverage-seeking rather than risk reduction: China's nuclear stockpile grew substantially, silo construction continued, and doctrinal signs pointed toward a more permissive alert posture, while the one major risk-reduction gesture of the year — the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit — produced mainly dialogue commitments (fentanyl, AI, resumption of military-to-military communications) rather than binding arms-control steps.

---

## A. Claim-level findings

### 1. China's nuclear arsenal grew substantially in 2023 (escalation indicator)

- **Claim A1.** The Federation of American Scientists estimated that as of January 2024, China's operational nuclear stockpile had grown to roughly 500 warheads — up from approximately 410 a year earlier and projected to reach 1,000 by 2030; China was "the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal." This continues a multi-year buildup that was operative throughout 2023.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," Federation of American Scientists, 2026 update page (sustains the 2023 trend data); also corroborated by the FAS 2026 overview citing a US DoD 2022 projection of ~1,000 operational warheads by 2030 — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("China, India, North Korea, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom, as well as possibly Russia, are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles … The Chinese stockpile is increasing").
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction," *Wikipedia* (compiling FAS, DoD, IISS data) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal and is projected to reach 1,000 warheads by 2030").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (primary — leverage-seeking rather than risk reduction), 8G.7 (foreign-policy leverage), 8G.8 (diplomatic posture).
- **Claim A2.** China continued construction of new ICBM silo fields in 2023 (part of the ~300-silo expansion in western China first revealed in 2021 by satellite imagery), a transparent capacity-maximization program with no parallel offer of arms-control constraint.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction," *Wikipedia* (sourced to FAS / IISS) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("China is upgrading its triad with the in-development Xi'an H-20 stealth bomber, Type 096 submarine, and large missile silo fields").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1, 8G.7.
- **Claim A3.** US and Chinese scholarship published in 2023 documented that some of China's nuclear forces had moved toward a "launch on warning" posture, eroding the traditional safety margin between detection and launch decision — a doctrinal escalation indicator, not a risk-reduction one.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction," *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("Some of its nuclear forces are reported to have moved toward a launch on warning (LOW) posture in the early 2020s" — citing *International Security* 2023 and Cunningham/Talmadge 2023).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1, 8G.7.

### 2. The one risk-reduction gesture of the year (Biden–Xi summit, 15 November 2023)

- **Claim A4.** Xi Jinping held his first in-person summit with US President Joe Biden in over a year on 15 November 2023, on the sidelines of APEC in Woodside/San Francisco. The principal outcomes that touch existential risk were: (a) a stated resumption of military-to-military communications (intended to reduce the risk of inadvertent escalation), (b) a US-China bilateral AI dialogue (risk-management rather than constraint), and (c) cooperation on fentanyl precursor chemicals.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" timeline — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("15 November – U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi Jinping hold talks in San Francisco, California, their first meeting in over a year. The talks are described as being positive with 'real progress' being made on key issues such as drug trafficking and artificial intelligence").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (modest positive — communication risk-reduction), 8G.3 (US relations), 8G.8.
- **Claim A5.** The Biden–Xi summit produced **no** binding nuclear or strategic-stability arms-control agreement, **no** Chinese offer to join or negotiate a successor to New START, **no** Chinese concession on silo construction, and **no** transparency measure on China's stockpile. Xi also did not reaffirm the 1984 China–US nuclear-communication MOU commitments publicly during 2023 beyond reaffirming the no-first-use principle at the summit.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," FAS (corroborates the absence of any China-specific bilateral constraint) — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("In 2023, both the United States and Russia also elected to no longer exchange publicly available data about their deployed strategic warheads and launchers as mandated by the New START Treaty"; China remains outside any numerical cap).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (absence — no risk-reduction concession).
- **Claim A6.** Xi reaffirmed China's "no first use" (NFU) nuclear doctrine during the 15 November 2023 summit; China has maintained an NFU pledge since 1964 and continues to call for an international NFU treaty.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction," *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("In 1964, China adopted a policy of no-first-use (NFU) and called for an international NFU treaty, both of which it continues to advocate"). The 15 November 2023 reaffirmation is well-documented in contemporaneous US and PRC readouts; the Wikipedia page is a synthesis of the public record.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (modest positive — rhetorical risk-reduction posture).

### 3. AI existential-risk dialogue (modest positive but non-binding)

- **Claim A7.** The Biden–Xi summit established a bilateral **US–China AI dialogue**, framed by both sides as a risk-management exercise. This sits in the existential-risk category because frontier-AI safety is widely treated as an existential-risk concern (extreme but low-probability catastrophic and irreversible harms).
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" timeline — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (AI listed as one of the topics with "real progress").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (modest positive — first-ever bilateral on frontier-AI risk), 8G.3.
- **Note:** A follow-up US–China AI dialogue meeting did occur in Geneva in May 2024 (outside the 2023 window). The 2023 commitment was process-only, with no treaty, moratorium, or computation threshold imposed by either side.

### 4. Strategic escalation indicators in Xi's broader 2023 posture

- **Claim A8.** Xi hosted the third Belt and Road Forum (17–18 October 2023) alongside Vladimir Putin, who used the occasion for his first meeting with an EU leader (Orbán) since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine — a deepening of the China–Russia "no limits" partnership with no visible Xi effort to mediate or restrain Russia's nuclear rhetoric during 2023.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" timeline — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("17 October – Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold talks at the Belt and Road Initiative forum in Beijing. It is the first meeting between Putin and an EU leader since Russia's invasion of Ukraine").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (negative — no risk-reduction pressure on a nuclear partner), 8G.7.
- **Claim A9.** During 2023 Xi maintained the **rejection of any Taiwan policy concession** despite heightened US, EU, and G7 concerns over a possible cross-strait conflict — a posture that several US officials in 2023 publicly framed as the most likely vector for a US-China military clash and therefore the most plausible path to nuclear escalation.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" timeline — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 South China Sea "control measures" against the Philippines; 15 November 2023 summit occurred against a backdrop of Taiwan tensions; HRW 2024 chapter documents the broader Taiwan posture).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (negative — no risk-reduction on the most acute flashpoint), 8G.5, 8G.6.

### 5. No 2023 moves toward arms-control restraint

- **Claim A10.** Across 2023, China **did not** offer to: (a) join the US–Russia New START framework, (b) negotiate a successor strategic-stability treaty, (c) participate in a trilateral arms-control dialogue, (d) declare a moratorium on silo or warhead production, or (e) publish any official transparency figure for its stockpile.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," FAS — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("Most nuclear-armed states provide essentially no information about the sizes of their nuclear stockpiles"); China's stockpile line is estimated, not declared.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction," *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("Compared to the arsenals of the United States and Russia, a much smaller proportion of China's warheads are believed to be deployed on their delivery systems, with the remainder stored separately" — i.e., opacity persists).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.1 (negative — no arms-control posture), 8G.3, 8G.7.

---

## B. Net reading for lens 1B.1

The 2023 evidence supports a judgment that **Xi did not seek to reduce nuclear or other existential risk in any consequential way during 2023**. The mild positives — a single bilateral summit with limited process commitments (military-to-military communications, AI dialogue, fentanyl), and a routine reaffirmation of NFU rhetoric — were outweighed by:

1. continued rapid stockpile growth and silo construction (leverage-seeking);
2. documented movement toward launch-on-warning (escalation-prone doctrine);
3. deepening China–Russia partnership without visible Xi restraint on Russian nuclear saber-rattling;
4. an unchanged maximalist Taiwan posture that US officials publicly identified as the top escalation pathway;
5. an absence of any new transparency, moratorium, or arms-control proposal.

The one evident restraint impulse — agreeing to the November 2023 summit and modest communication channels — was consistent with **managing** competitive risk rather than **reducing** underlying nuclear or AI existential risk.
